# Tabular data with pandas

One file in this book's data folder is 513,592 bytes and holds 27,179 rows of
whole numbers, one row per mouse gene, across twelve sample columns. Nothing
inside it says what those numbers count or which animal each column came from.
So here's the question you can't answer yet: does 939 in one column beat 759 in
another? That has an answer, and it isn't the obvious one.

The file is `data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz`. It came out of the Gene Expression
Omnibus, or GEO, which is NCBI's public archive of expression data, under the
accession `GSE60450`. Twelve samples of mouse mammary gland went into it.
Chapter 3 told you where the book's data folder lives, and Chapters 21, 24 and
25 all come back to this one file.

## Open it before you believe anything about it

Every file you've handled so far held one sequence at a time, and Python's
string tools were the right shape for that. A table isn't that shape. It has
named columns, it has rows, and each column holds one kind of thing all the way
down. The library everybody uses for tables in Python is called pandas, and the
table it gives you is a
[DataFrame]{.term def="A table in pandas. Named columns, numbered rows, and one kind of value in each column."}.

Read the file and ask it how big it is.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

counts = pd.read_csv("data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz", sep="\t")
print(counts.shape)
```

Two things happened without you asking for them. The file ends in `.gz`, so
pandas uncompressed it on the way in. And `sep="\t"` says the columns are
separated by tab characters, which is what the `.tsv` in the name means.

Check the shape before you look at anything else. Rows first, then columns:
27,179 genes across 14 columns, twelve of which are samples. Leave `sep="\t"`
out and pandas assumes commas, finds none in a tab-separated file, and hands you
27,179 rows of a single column. No error, no warning, nothing red. The shape is
how you catch it.

Now look at what the columns are called.

```{python}
for name in counts.columns[:4]:
    print(name)
```

Those are the two that aren't samples. Here `EntrezGeneID` names the gene and
`Length` is how long that gene is in bases, which you'll want in a moment.
The remaining twelve are the samples, and
their names have collected debris. Everything after the first underscore is
bookkeeping from the sequencing machine, down to which lane of which flowcell
each read came off. Only the part in front of the first underscore names the
tube, and only that part will match anything else you own.

```{python}
counts.columns = [name.split("_")[0] for name in counts.columns]
print(counts.columns[2:8].tolist())
print(counts.columns[8:].tolist())
```

The square brackets hold a loop written on one line. It says: for every name in
`counts.columns`, cut the name at the first underscore and keep the front piece.
The list that comes out replaces the old column names, and you'll see the same
line at the top of every chapter that opens this file.

Six names starting `MCL1-D`, then six starting `MCL1-L`. Hold on to that
ordering. It matters later in this chapter and it matters a lot in Chapter 24.

```{python}
print(counts[["EntrezGeneID", "MCL1-DG", "MCL1-LA"]].head())
```

A list of column names inside the square brackets gives you those columns and
drops the rest. `.head()` gives you the first five rows. The numbers on the
left, `0` through `4`, are pandas numbering the rows for you. They aren't in
the file.

## What one of these numbers is, and what it isn't

Each number is a count of sequencing reads. Somebody broke the RNA in one
sample into millions of short pieces, read them, worked out which gene each
piece came from, and tallied the result. A `438` in the `MCL1-DG` column means
438 reads from that sample landed on that gene. A table shaped like this one, a
row per gene and a column per sample, is what everybody calls a count matrix.

Each count carries two things at once: how much of the gene the cell was
making, and how hard somebody looked. Add up a column and you get the second
one on its own. The sum of one sample's column is its
[library size]{.term def="The total number of reads counted in one sample. It is the sum of that sample's column."},
the number of reads it contributed.

```{python}
sample_cols = list(counts.columns[2:])
library_size = counts[sample_cols].sum()
print(library_size.sort_values())
```

`.sum()` on a set of columns adds each one up and hands back one number per
column. Then `.sort_values()` puts them in order, smallest first, which is the
fast way to see a range.

The shallowest sample is `MCL1-DL` at 20,015,386 reads. The deepest is
`MCL1-LE` at 24,723,827. Divide the second by the first and you get 1.235.
Sequencing went about a quarter further on `MCL1-LE`, and every gene in that
column collects about a quarter more counts for nothing.

<!-- nlr-allow: 11974 -->

Watch it happen on one gene. Here is gene 11974 in those two columns.

```{python}
row = counts["EntrezGeneID"] == 11974
print(counts.loc[row, ["MCL1-DL", "MCL1-LE"]])
```

939 against 759 looks like a real difference. Work out the ratio: 939 divided
by 759 is 1.237. You got 1.235 out of the library sizes a moment ago. Those
two numbers agree to three digits, and that agreement is the whole story.

### Counts per million, derived here

The fix is division. Take each count, divide it by the total of its own column,
and you have that gene's share of that sample. Those shares are tiny, so
multiply by a million to get numbers you can read out loud. That's
[counts per million]{.term def="A raw count divided by its own sample's library size, times a million. It makes one gene comparable across samples."},
written CPM from here on.

```{python}
cpm = counts[sample_cols] / library_size * 1e6
print(cpm.loc[row, ["MCL1-DL", "MCL1-LE"]].round(1))
```

37.9 and 38.0. The gap closed. Two counts 180 apart turn out to be the same
gene sitting at the same level in both samples, and the whole difference was
how deep the sequencing went.

That division works because `library_size` carries the column names as its
labels. When you divide, pandas matches those labels against the columns of the
table instead of going by position. This is the first of two places in this
chapter where that habit saves you.

<!-- nlr-allow: 1000000 -->

::: {.check}
Run `print(cpm.sum().round(0))`. Every one of the twelve columns should read
`1000000.0`. No coincidence, and no rounding artifact either: you divided each
column by its own total, so each column sums to a million by construction. If
one column reads something else, you divided by the wrong thing.
:::

CPM fixes the column and does nothing at all to the row, and that's the limit
you have to carry from here. Remember the `Length` column. A gene twice as long
catches about twice as many reads at the same true expression, because there's
twice as much of it to break into pieces. So you can compare one gene across
the twelve columns, which is what the rest of this book does. You can't line
two different genes up inside one column and say which is expressed more.

::: {.why}
Chapter 7 said an E-value means nothing without the size of the database behind
it. This is the same shape of problem in a different costume. A count means
nothing without the library size behind it, and the count is printed in the
file while the library size is not. Any number you meet in this field is worth
one question before you write it down: divided by what?
:::

## The row labels are integers on purpose

Look back at that first column. `EntrezGeneID` holds an
[Entrez Gene ID]{.term def="NCBI's permanent integer identifier for one gene in one species. Stable and unique, and it tells you nothing on sight."},
and every value in it is a whole number. You cannot tell what gene 11974 is by
looking at it. That's the trade the file made.

An Entrez ID is stable. It's assigned once, it points at one gene in one
species forever, and no committee is going to change it while your analysis is
running. The IDs are unique too, so two rows carrying the same one would be a
defect rather than an ambiguity.

A gene symbol is the opposite trade. `Brca1` is readable and 12189 isn't, and
that's the entire case for symbols. Against them, the list runs longer. Symbols
get retired and reissued by nomenclature committees. The same symbol has meant
different genes in different years. Human and mouse committees capitalize
differently, which is why Chapter 5 had you write `BRCA1` and `Brca1` as two
separate strings. A comparison between those two fails silently.

::: {.trap}
Open a gene list in a spreadsheet and some of the symbols stop being symbols.
SEPT7 becomes a date in September. MARCH1 becomes a date in March, and DEC1
goes the same way in December. The program doesn't ask you, doesn't flag it,
and writes the dates back out when you save. Mark Ziemann and colleagues found
this in 704 of 3,597 papers with Excel gene lists in 2016. The same group
counted again in 2021, after five years of public warnings, and found it in
3,436 of 11,117, which is 30.9 percent. The rate went up. The HUGO Gene
Nomenclature Committee has since renamed the symbols that kept getting eaten,
so SEPT7 is now SEPTIN7 and MARCH1 is MARCHF1. Renaming the genes turned out to
be the easier fix, which tells you something about the other one.
:::

No spreadsheet turns 12189 into a date. That's why this file ships integers. The
mapping from ID to name belongs at the end, on a short results table, rather
than at the start on all 27,179 rows. Chapter 24 does that mapping once there's
something worth naming.

## Keeping the rows you want

Most of those 27,179 rows are dead weight. Plenty of them are zero in every one
of the twelve columns. Plenty more sit at one or two reads, where the number
tells you about luck rather than about the tissue. So the first thing anybody
does with a count matrix is throw rows away, on a rule stated out loud.

```{python}
print((counts[sample_cols].sum(axis=1) == 0).sum(), "rows are zero everywhere")
expressed = counts[(cpm >= 1).sum(axis=1) >= 3]
print(len(counts), "rows in")
print(len(expressed), "rows out")
```

Read that condition from the inside out. The comparison `cpm >= 1` builds a
table of True and False the same shape as `cpm`. Every True counts as 1, so
`.sum(axis=1)` runs along each row and gives you how many samples cleared the
bar. A row survives `>= 3` when that number is three or more, and `counts[...]`
keeps the survivors.

One word in there decides everything. `axis=1` means along the row, and
`axis=0`, the default, means down the column. Get those two the wrong way round
and the code runs cleanly and answers a question you didn't ask, so say the
direction out loud each time you type it.

Nearly half the rows are gone, and the rule that dropped them isn't free. A
gene that clears 1 CPM in only two of the twelve samples goes out with the
rest, however loudly it fires in those two. This study puts only two samples in
some of its groups. The rule is one somebody chose, it isn't a law, and Chapter
24 uses this exact one so that the numbers there match the numbers here.

## Which sample is which column

`MCL1-DG` is a tube. It doesn't say whether that tube held basal cells or
luminal cells, or whether the mouse was virgin, pregnant or lactating. None of
that is in the count matrix. It lives in a second file.

```{python}
samples = pd.read_csv("data/GSE60450_samples.csv")
print(samples[["sample", "gsm", "cell_type", "stage"]].head(4))
```

Twelve rows, one per sample. The `gsm` column holds the GEO accession for each
one, which is the identifier you'd quote in a paper.

Now put the two tables together. Here's how it goes the first time, for almost
everybody. Take the sample table in accession order, walk down the columns of
the count matrix, and hand out the labels as you go.

```{python}
by_accession = samples.sort_values("gsm")
guess = pd.DataFrame({"column": sample_cols,
                      "cell_type": list(by_accession["cell_type"])})
print(guess)
```

Read the result. `MCL1-DG` comes out luminal, and so do the next five. Then all
six `MCL1-L` columns come out basal.

All twelve are wrong. They're wrong consistently, which is the most expensive
way to be wrong. The count matrix runs its six basal samples first and its six
luminal samples second. The GEO accessions run the other way round. Accession
`GSM1480291` belongs to `MCL1-LA`, which is the seventh of the twelve sample
columns rather than the first.

::: {.trap}
Nothing above raised an error. Both lists held twelve entries, pandas set them
side by side without a word, and printed a tidy table. Every number you
computed downstream would be a real number, correctly calculated, about the
wrong samples. Chapter 24 makes this exact mistake on the full dataset, catches
it with a gene whose answer was already known, and recovers. Watch for it
there.
:::

### Join on a key instead

A key is a column whose values name the rows, so `sample` is the key here and
`MCL1-DG` is one of its values. Both tables have to carry it. Build the second
table so it does.

```{python}
totals = pd.DataFrame({"sample": sample_cols,
                       "library_size": library_size.values})
design = totals.merge(samples, on="sample")
print(design[["sample", "gsm", "cell_type", "stage"]])
```

`merge` looks up each value of `sample` in the other table and brings the
matching row across. Where that row happens to sit doesn't enter into it. Prove
that to yourself: merge again against the accession-ordered copy and compare
the answers.

```{python}
again = totals.merge(by_accession, on="sample")
print(again["cell_type"].equals(design["cell_type"]))
```

::: {.check}
`MCL1-DG` must come out `basal` and `MCL1-LA` must come out `luminal`. If
you've got that pair the other way round, you joined by position. One more
thing worth knowing. Had you merged before trimming those column names,
`MCL1-DG_BC2CTUACXX_ACTTGA_L002_R1` would have matched nothing on the other
side. You'd have got back a table with zero rows and no complaint. Check the
row count of anything you merge.
:::

### One number per group

`groupby` splits a table into piles according to the values in one or more
columns, then computes something for each pile. Part 4 leans on it constantly.

```{python}
print(design.groupby(["cell_type", "stage"])["library_size"].mean())
```

Six piles. Two cell types, three stages, two samples in each combination. That's
the whole design of the experiment, and you read it off your own table instead
of off somebody's methods section.

Now read the numbers next to the piles. The lowest mean and the second highest
are both basal. The highest and the second lowest are both luminal. So nobody
sequenced one cell type harder than the other, and the depth differences you
found earlier look like run-to-run variation rather than something built into
the study. You had no way of knowing that before you looked.

## Exercises

<!-- nlr-allow: 12993 12991 12990 11475 20750 -->

::: {.exercise num="20.1" time="40 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Rank all 27,179 genes by how much they vary across the twelve samples, once on
CPM and once on the raw counts, then say what changed between the two rankings.
:::
::: {.given}
`counts`, `cpm` and `sample_cols` as this chapter built them. Use the standard
deviation across the twelve sample columns as the measure of variation, which
is `.std(axis=1)`. Rank all rows, with no filtering step.
:::
::: {.produce}
Two ordered lists of ten Entrez Gene IDs, most variable first, plus one number:
how many of the ten appear in both lists.
:::
::: {.check}
Both lists open 12993, 12991, 12990, and all ten IDs appear in both, so your
number is ten. Exactly one adjacent pair trades places: 11475 is eighth on CPM
and ninth on the raw counts, and 20750 does the reverse. That pair is the whole
effect. Look at 20750's counts across the twelve columns and you'll see why it
slips. It peaks in `MCL1-LE` and `MCL1-LF`, the two deepest columns in the
file, so normalizing takes something off it. If your two lists disagree
on more than that pair, print `cpm.sum()` and confirm each column is a million
before you go any further.
:::

::: {.answerbox height="2.4in"}
:::
:::

Then the part that isn't in the answer. Those two rankings barely differ, and
the reason is the range you measured earlier: 20,015,386 reads to 24,723,827,
a spread of about a quarter. Run the same ranking on a study where one sample
came back at half the depth of another and the two lists come apart. Nothing in
either list tells you which situation you're in. Which is why you normalize
first, every time, instead of checking afterwards whether it mattered.

Take one more minute at the end. Look up 12993 in NCBI Gene the way Chapter 5
showed you, and see whether the answer fits animals that were lactating.

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="KeyError: 'MCL1-DG'"}
pandas is talking, and it's telling you there's no column by that name. You
asked for the short name before running the cell that trimmed the column names,
so the real name is still `MCL1-DG_BC2CTUACXX_ACTTGA_L002_R1`. Print
`counts.columns[:4]` to see which version you're holding.
:::

::: {.errfix err="NameError: name 'cpm' is not defined"}
Python is talking, and no table is involved. The cell that built `cpm` hasn't
run in this session. Colab throws away everything when the runtime restarts, so
after a disconnect you have to run the cells above again. Restart and run all
is the reliable version of that.
:::

::: {.errfix err="FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz'"}
Python looked in the folder your notebook is standing in and found no `data`
folder under it. Either the file went away when the runtime recycled, or you're
a folder off. List the current folder's contents before you retype the path.
:::

::: {.errfix err="KeyError: 'sample_name'"}
You gave `merge` a key that isn't a column in both tables. `on=` takes the name
of a column that exists on each side, spelled identically. Print the column
names of both tables and compare them character by character.
:::
:::
